lesson.title: Taming a River, Powering a Region: The Tennessee Valley Authority
lesson.summary: Created in May 1933, the Tennessee Valley Authority built dams across the Tennessee River system to control flooding, generate electricity, and bring economic development to one of the poorest regions in the country.
lesson.body:
The Tennessee Valley, spanning parts of Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Kentucky, Georgia, North Carolina, and Virginia, was among the poorest and least electrified regions in the country, and it suffered regular, destructive flooding. A federal nitrate and hydroelectric facility built at Muscle Shoals, Alabama during World War One had sat partly unused for years while Congress argued over whether the government or private utilities should control it.

Roosevelt resolved that argument by creating an entirely new kind of federal agency. He signed the Tennessee Valley Authority Act on May 18, 1933, establishing a government owned corporation with the authority to plan development across the whole river system: building dams for flood control and navigation, generating and selling electricity, and replanting eroded hillsides. Norris Dam, completed in 1936, was the first of many built under the program.

The TVA brought electricity to rural farms and towns that private power companies had judged too costly and unprofitable to serve, transforming daily life for families who had never had electric lighting, refrigeration, or powered farm equipment. It also created large numbers of construction jobs at the height of the Depression, though private utility companies fought its expansion as unfair government competition.

The TVA still operates today, a rare American example of a regional planning authority. It stands as one of the clearest illustrations of a broader New Deal idea: that some infrastructure projects were simply too large and too unprofitable for private industry to undertake alone, and that only the federal government had the resources and reach to attempt them.
